displayQuote: Remember, George, this is no time to go wobbly

meta.title: Who really said "Remember, George, this is no time to go wobbly"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Thatcher really did tell Bush not to go wobbly, in a 1990 phone call about Kuwait. The famous “Remember, George” opening is not in the record.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Remember, George, this is no time to go wobbly'?
meta.ogDescription: Real remark, real phone call, August 1990 — but the two words that make the quote famous appear in none of the documented versions.

answer.label: Margaret Thatcher — but not in these words
answer.sourceLine: Thatcher did say it, and the occasion is well established: a telephone conversation with President George H. W. Bush on 26 August 1990, weeks after Iraq invaded Kuwait, when Bush was hesitating over the scale of the response. What is not established is the wording people quote. Wikipedia’s account of the Anglo-American relationship ↗ renders it “this is no time to go wobbly,” citing Bush and Scowcroft’s A World Transformed (p. 352) and Thatcher’s own The Downing Street Years (pp. 823–24). Its foreign-relations article ↗ gives “This was no time to go wobbly!” and the Gulf War article ↗ has her “urging Bush not to go wobbly.” None of the three opens with “Remember, George.”

source.heading: The phone call, and three renderings of it

docMeta.dd: Three weeks after Iraq’s invasion of Kuwait; Bush was weighing the scale of the US response.
Thatcher, The Downing Street Years (1993), pp. 823–24; Bush & Scowcroft, A World Transformed (1998), p. 352 — both cited by Wikipedia.
“Remember, George” — absent from every scholarly rendering found.

source.excerpt: This is no time to go wobbly.
trail: Read the raw wikitext of the Wikiquote Margaret Thatcher page ↗. “Remember, George, this is no time to go wobbly” appears in the Disputed section, sourced only to an Associated Press story published 8 March 1991 — months after the call itself.

Wikiquote also records that Dick Cheney called the quotation “an old wives’ story” ↗ in a 2013 interview, and that PolitiFact reviewed the available source material and rated Cheney’s claim False. PolitiFact itself is blocked by this run’s network policy, so that verdict is reported here as Wikiquote records it, not as a page we read.

Cross-checked three Wikipedia articles that cite the primary memoirs: Special Relationship ↗ (“this is no time to go wobbly”), History of the foreign relations of the United Kingdom ↗ (“This was no time to go wobbly!”, dated 26 August 1990) and Gulf War ↗ (“not to go wobbly”). Not one includes “Remember, George.”

Tried to read the two memoirs directly. Both A World Transformed ↗ and Thatcher’s The Downing Street Years are on the Internet Archive as lending-restricted scans and returned an authorisation error, so their exact pages remain unverified here.
source.excerptNote: That is the form Wikipedia uses when citing the two memoirs directly. Both memoirs are lending-restricted scans that could not be opened in this run, so the sentence above is the encyclopaedia’s rendering of them rather than a reading of either page. The variation across three Wikipedia articles — “this is,” “This was,” “not to” — is itself the point: even careful secondary sources do not agree on the exact words.

sourceLink.text: Wikipedia: Special Relationship (Thatcher and George H. W. Bush)

source.rightsNote: No rights status is asserted. The underlying remark was spoken in a private 1990 telephone call and reaches us only through later published accounts — a 1991 news report and two memoirs of 1993 and 1998, all firmly in copyright. There is no public-domain text here, and the exact wording quoted has no identified published source of its own.

author.name: Margaret Thatcher
author.heading: About Margaret Thatcher
author.bio: Margaret Thatcher was Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1979 to 1990. The Kuwait crisis caught her at the very end of that run — she was out of office by November 1990, and the Gulf War began in January 1991 under John Major. Her intervention with Bush in August 1990 is among the most cited moments of the Anglo-American relationship, which is exactly the kind of story that acquires a better script over time. “Don’t go wobbly” is hers. The stage direction in front of it is not.

cite.sourceCitation: Remark made in a Bush–Thatcher telephone conversation, 26 August 1990, during the Kuwait crisis. Documented accounts: Margaret Thatcher, The Downing Street Years (London: HarperCollins, 1993), 823–24; George H. W. Bush and Brent Scowcroft, A World Transformed (New York: Knopf, 1998), 352 — both as cited by Wikipedia, which renders the remark “this is no time to go wobbly.” The popular “Remember, George” opening appears in none of these renderings.
cite.pageCitation: Quotle.info. “Who really said ‘Remember, George, this is no time to go wobbly’?” Last verified 20 Aug 2026.

copyAttribution: Right person, embellished words. "Remember, George, this is no time to go wobbly." — Margaret Thatcher really did urge President George H. W. Bush not to go wobbly, in a telephone call on 26 August 1990 during the Kuwait crisis. But the documented renderings, in her memoir The Downing Street Years (1993) and in Bush and Scowcroft's A World Transformed (1998), run simply "this is no time to go wobbly." The "Remember, George" opening is not in the record. Traced by Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: What was added, and when
misattribution.intro: This is not a fake quotation. It is a real one that grew a stage direction — two words that turn a line from a phone call into a scene with a cast.

items.why: Three separate Wikipedia articles citing the primary memoirs render the remark without it: “this is no time to go wobbly” ↗, “This was no time to go wobbly!” ↗ and “not to go wobbly” ↗.

items.scope: Where the popular version is sourced
items.why: Wikiquote’s Disputed section ↗ traces the “Remember, George” wording to an AP story published more than six months after the conversation — a report of a remark, not a transcript of one.

items.scope: The denial that did not hold
items.why: Cheney called the quotation “an old wives’ story” in 2013. Wikiquote records that PolitiFact reviewed the source material and rated that claim False — the substance of the remark stands, whatever the exact words were.

misattribution.truthLine: So: she said it, he was the one she said it to, and the crisis was real. If you are quoting her, quote the documented form ↗ — “this is no time to go wobbly” — and leave the stage direction out.

context.heading: Why this line mattered
lead: Iraq invaded Kuwait on 2 August 1990. Thatcher happened to be in the United States at the time, and over the following weeks she pressed a hesitant Bush administration towards a firm response — reminding the President, as Wikipedia’s Gulf War article puts it, that appeasement in the 1930s had led to war, and that Saddam Hussein would otherwise have the Gulf and much of the world’s oil supply at his mercy.

The “wobbly” remark became the shorthand for that whole intervention: the moment a British Prime Minister is said to have stiffened an American President’s spine. It is a good story, and good stories get tightened. The version with “Remember, George” in front of it is the tightened one.
context.detailsSummary: What this run could not read
detailsBody: Three sources that bear directly on this quotation are blocked by the network policy in force for this run: the Margaret Thatcher Foundation archive (which holds the commentary page on the Bush–Thatcher call), PolitiFact’s fact-check of Cheney’s denial, and the Internet Archive’s wayback service. The two memoirs are on the Internet Archive but lending-restricted.

Everything asserted above therefore rests on sources that were read in full: the raw wikitext of Wikiquote’s Thatcher page and three Wikipedia articles that cite the memoirs by page number. Where a claim originates with PolitiFact or the AP, this page says so rather than implying it was checked at source.
context.pull: She said it. He was the one she said it to. The two words that make it a scene were added later.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote places "Remember, George, this is no time to go wobbly." in its Disputed section, sourced to an AP story published 8 March 1991, records Dick Cheney calling it "an old wives' story" in a 2013 Fox News interview, and records that PolitiFact rated Cheney's claim False.

Wikipedia's Special Relationship article states that in the midst of the invasion of Kuwait, Thatcher advised Bush that "this is no time to go wobbly", citing Bush & Scowcroft, A World Transformed (1998), p. 352 and Thatcher, The Downing Street Years (1993), pp. 823-24.

Wikipedia's History of the foreign relations of the United Kingdom article states Bush was apprehensive, prompting Thatcher to remark during a telephone conversation that "This was no time to go wobbly!", citing a Margaret Thatcher Foundation document dated 26 August 1990.
Wikipedia's Gulf War article describes Thatcher reminding Bush of 1930s appeasement and of Saddam holding 65% of the world's oil supply at his mercy, and "famously urging Bush not to go wobbly".
Margaret Thatcher was born 13 October 1925 and died 8 April 2013; she was Prime Minister until November 1990.
